Another affected setup — this one demonstrates the **web-UI-specific consequences** of the same root cause (opencode 1.18.16, Linux, `opencode web`).

## Root cause (verified on disk + live API)

Renamed project folder `…/steuerberater` → `…/steuerberaterin`. The `project` row keeps `worktree = …/steuerberater` (stale) while `sandboxes` and the `project_directory` table correctly point to `…/steuerberaterin`. All session rows also correctly store `directory = …/steuerberaterin`. Only `project.worktree` is stale.

## Web-specific symptoms

1. **`GET /project/current` returns the stale `worktree`** — the web homepage resolves a path that does not exist, so it looks like the project is "not detected".

2. **Every "New Session" recreates the dead folder.** New sessions are created at the stale `worktree` path. opencode `mkdir`s the missing directory and bootstraps `.opencode/` there — creating `package.json` with `{"dependencies": {"@opencode-ai/plugin": "1.18.16"}}`, `node_modules/`, and plugin state (`goals/` from the goal plugin). `rm -rf` of the recreated folder does **not** help: the next new session recreates it.

3. **New sessions silently fall back to the `global` project.** Because the stale path is not a git repo, those sessions get `project_id = global`, `directory = <stale path>`. So the project's session list in the web UI stays empty / wrong, while the real sessions (100+ rows, `directory = <renamed path>`, same `project_id`) remain invisible in the UI even though the API serves them fine.

## Live evidence

- `GET /project/current` →
  `{"worktree": "…/steuerberater", "sandboxes": ["…/steuerberaterin"]}`
- `GET /session` → all sessions carry the project's `id` and `directory = …/steuerberaterin` — data intact, just unreachable through the stale worktree.
- `PATCH /project/{projectID}` only updates `name`/`icon`/`commands` (per OpenAPI spec) — **there is no self-service API to repair the stale `worktree`**.

## Workaround

```sql
-- stop the server first
UPDATE project SET worktree='<renamed path>' WHERE id='<projectID>';
```

Then restart `opencode web` from the renamed folder and delete the recreated dead folder.

I am seeing the same general failure pattern, including internal-looking text leaking into the TUI and compaction not completing.

My environment:

- OpenCode `1.18.16`
- macOS `25.6.0` on arm64
- Terminals: Ghostty `1.3.1` and the Zed integrated terminal
- Session ID: `ses_00a38fe1cffef3fdfqdS44708e`
- Models tested: Claude Sonnet and Haiku through AWS Bedrock and `deepseek-v4-flash` through OpenCode Zen Free.

The issue appeared across both Ghostty and Zed, and across more than one provider, so it does not look specific to one terminal. When compaction triggered, the TUI started showing a large amount of internal/reasoning-like text and the compaction state did not finish. The session could remain stuck with the compaction indicator active.

The example in my debug output showed text such as `Thought: 16.5s`, followed by internal planning text and tool-call payloads being displayed in the TUI. This looked similar to the behavior described in this issue, although my report also includes the compaction hang.

I then retried compacting the same session using `deepseek-v4-flash` through the native DeepSeek API instead of OpenCode Zen, and that compaction completed successfully. This suggests there may be an interaction with the OpenCode/Zen route or with the compaction request format, rather than a terminal-only problem or a general inability of the session to compact.

As a temporary mitigation, I am testing the compaction agent with reasoning disabled.

Runtime verification (reported by PR author):

Tested on OpenCode Desktop 1.18.16 (Windows) with opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash (1M context). The same prompt-layout patch was applied directly to the Desktop bundle (app.asar) for testing.

Result: a ~350K-token session that previously would not compact correctly (the model answered an old question from the conversation instead of summarizing) now produces the proper anchored summary (## Objective / ## Important Details / ## Work State / ## Next Move / ## Relevant Files) via /compact.

This confirms the ordering fix resolves the reported behavior on the exact model/stack from #41801.

Additional measurement data from a Windows 11 setup running 7 local stdio MCPs + 6 remote MCPs in opencode.jsonc:

**Cold-start, one-at-a-time (sequential probe via Node spawn + JSON-RPC initialize):**
- memory 1256ms, postgres 538ms, mysql 1727ms, sqlite 1468ms, sequential-thinking 1226ms, playwright 1190ms, fetch 5271ms
- All under 6s alone. No single server is slow enough to explain a timeout.

**Cold-start, all 7 spawned simultaneously (same probe):**
- FULLY READY AFTER: 7320ms (postgres 1819ms … fetch 7320ms)
- Even under parallel spawn the slowest (fetch, python 3.14) finishes in ~7s.

So locally the parallel spawn does NOT reliably reproduce on this machine — but the observed flakiness matches your description ("different MCPs fail on each run"): under a real desktop startup the failure set is non-deterministic, consistent with a spawn-order/stdio-close race rather than any single server being slow.

One environment note that interacts with this: several of our remote MCPs (cloudflare-*) had just-expired OAuth access tokens at desktop startup, and the startup logs showed `server unavailable ... status=failed` batches — remote auth failure and the parallel spawn race can compound (a remote that needs a token refresh occupies the handshake longer, widening the window for local stdio servers to get killed/closed mid-initialize).

Repro loop (`opencode mcp list` x3, grep -c fail|error) would likely show the intermittent failures here too. If a fix PR needs a stress repro, happy to run the loop against a build.

This is FM-007, lost-context, but happening at the framework level instead of the agent level — compression is discarding the anchor that everything else depends on.

The issue quotes the mechanism precisely: "Context compression discards the early conversation turns (initial user message + model's initial reasoning) while preserving only the most recent tool call results and model responses." That's a summarization strategy that treats all early turns as equally disposable, when the very first user turn is structurally different from the rest — it's the goal, not a step toward the goal. Everything downstream (the "该项目存在哪些EMB_REVIEW_MODE=auto_mode类似这种的环境变量" query, the parse of engine.groovy/nodes/init.py/directives.py) is scaffolding that exists to answer that one turn. Drop the anchor and the model doesn't fail loudly, it fails silently by pattern-matching on whatever tool output is still in window — hence the fabricated "feat(006)" commit summary that answers nothing.

The deterministic check: at the compression boundary, assert that turn[0] (or a verbatim/near-verbatim summary of it) is present in the post-compression context, and fail the compression step — not the generation step — if it isn't. This has to be a structural invariant on the compressor's output, not a runtime heuristic on the response. Concretely: `assert original_task_anchor in compressed_context`, checked before the compressed context is ever handed to the model, with the anchor computed once at turn 0 and pinned outside the sliding/compressible window entirely rather than re-derived from whatever survives summarization.

What would confirm or refute this: whether OpenCode's compression prompt/summarizer explicitly excludes turn 0 by design (confirms) or whether it's supposed to preserve it and something else (token budget bug, summarizer truncation) is dropping it silently (refutes my framing and points to an implementation bug instead of a design gap).

Advisory SFA-2026-C61227E523 · Full redacted write-up: https://impartshadow.github.io/echo-site/failure-cases/context-compression-loses-initial-user-question-and-c61227e523.html — I triage one of these in public
every day.
If this diagnosis is useful, react 👍 to this comment; if it is wrong, react 👎 — I use the verdict to choose what I investigate next.

I think I can answer the question in your last paragraph, with measurements rather than a guess: the Go purchase is almost certainly fine, and the request simply never reaches Go.

`opencode` (Zen) and `opencode-go` are two separate providers, and their model lists overlap by name — on my machine the local catalogue has 88 Zen models and 24 Go models, and **16 of those 24 Go models have an identically named twin in Zen**, including `glm-5.2`, `deepseek-v4-flash`, `kimi-k3` and `grok-4.5`. The picker shows the same string for both. Connecting the OpenCode Go provider does not move an existing session onto it: after connecting Go, my log still read `189 providerID=opencode / 0 providerID=opencode-go`. Zen `-free` models fail with the free-tier 429 that the UI renders as "Free usage exceeded, subscribe to Go" — hence the message telling Go subscribers to buy Go.

Picking the model from the **OpenCode Go** group fixed it here.

Your `retrying in 32969s - attempt #1` is the second half of it: when the failure lands during compaction, the session wedges — exponential backoff, survives app restarts, and ignores the model picker until you explicitly hit stop. Details and log excerpts in #42035.

Same symptom here, and it turned out not to be an account problem. `opencode` (Zen) and `opencode-go` are two different providers whose model names overlap — 16 of the 24 Go models have an identically named twin in Zen, so the picker shows e.g. `glm-5.2` twice, but only the Go one is covered by a Go subscription. Zen `-free` models hit the free-tier limit that the UI renders as "Free usage exceeded, subscribe to Go". After connecting Go my log still showed `189 providerID=opencode / 0 providerID=opencode-go` — the request never reached Go. Selecting the model from the **OpenCode Go** group fixed it.

If it happened while your session was compacting, you also have to press stop first: the retry loop survives app restarts and ignores the model picker until aborted. Measurements and log excerpts: #42035
